A Financial Times investigation has uncovered an extensive network allegedly moving billions of dollars in Nvidia ( $NVDA ) AI chips into China through Southeast Asia, linking former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to Chinese gaming companies, offshore entities and individuals associated with an alleged Cambodian criminal syndicate. The findings deepen scrutiny of Nvidia's export controls following Jensen Huang's resignation.

-  Chip Supply Network
The FT traced connections among Nvidia, U.S.-based server supplier Aivres, Singapore's Megaspeed and Chinese gaming and data-center companies. Aivres continued supplying Nvidia systems after its parent-linked company Inspur was placed on the U.S. Entity List in 2023.

-  $4.6B in Shipments
Trade records show Megaspeed's Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix imported approximately $4.6B in goods from Aivres between December 2024 and December 2025. Sources told the FT that many Nvidia chips ultimately reached China through Southeast Asian smuggling routes, although the full value diverted remains unverified.

-  Alice Huang's Connections
Huang acquired and renamed a Singapore subsidiary of gaming company 7Road in 2023, creating Megaspeed. Her family maintained investment ties to Century Huatong, whose affiliated companies allegedly helped distribute restricted Nvidia chips inside China.

-  Cambodian Crime Links
The FT identified indirect corporate connections to Hu Xiaowei, whom U.S. authorities accuse of involvement in Prince Group's alleged cyber-scam, money-laundering and smuggling operations. Prince Group disputes the allegations. The investigation does not establish that every connected company knowingly participated.

-  U.S. Investigation
Commerce began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 and requested Nvidia sales records in May 2025. Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its no-sell list in June 2025 and says it also restricted Aivres. The Justice Department subsequently assumed the lead in the criminal investigation.

-  Major Chinese Tech Firms
Tencent ( $TCEHY ) and Alibaba ( $BABA ) have investment or business ties to companies identified in the network. The FT found no evidence either participated in chip smuggling, and Tencent denied knowledge or involvement.

-  Export Control Concerns
The findings highlight how offshore companies, intermediaries and Southeast Asian data centers can complicate enforcement of U.S. AI chip restrictions. Washington has recently tightened controls on Chinese access to advanced computing through the region.

The investigation identifies corporate links and alleged diversion routes, not proof that Nvidia or every connected business knowingly facilitated illegal exports. Allegations involving Alice Huang and Chinese intelligence also remain unproven.

Great summary of the extraordinary progress that was made in AI over the past 2 years. If we only looked at the start and end of $NVDA as a representative of the value of a key input into AI economy, it might look as though everything had been anticipated. 

But $NVDA went from $132 on June 14, 2024 to a recent high of ~$239 on Oct 6, 2026. Not everything was priced in. Meanwhile in private markets, OpenAI went 15x higher, and Anthropic 85x higher. Clearly not everything was priced in!

Something fundamentally changed over the last two months or one can argue since the middle of the year, where most of the AI-adjacent names reached a local top since which we’ve had a couple counter-rallies. This is what happens when coming into this year the narrative of the AI trade became mainstream and well known to even the average person. Leverage and valuation accelerated baking in ever more aggressive assumptions. 

Solving Navier-Stokes and’s Riemann Hypothesis is impressive, monumental achievement even. But is it worth a lot economically to justify the investment input to allow us to achieve it? What’s the TAM of solving Millennium problems? Is there a simple extrapolation from such frontier capability to broad commercial applicability or is frontier AI still plagued by the “pyramid problem”, where the base of application shrinks at the top?

That is what the market is increasingly evaluating and concerned (vs the valuation baked in) now that the AI trade has gone from little known and widely doubted back in middle 2023, when it was a “baby bubble”, to end of 2026 where the trade is much more symmetric. You have little margin of safety. You win by actually predicting correctly what will happen. Back then you could ride on things just not being as bad/better than people thought.

quoted.text:
Flashback to June 14, 2024.

At the time, frontier AI models have zero fluid intelligence. They score around 5% on ARC 1. They can't reliably add two numbers. They make laughable logic errors every other prompt. Reasoning models don't exist. Coding agents don't exist. Claude Code doesn't exist. "Code gen" is a complete joke. Scaling up next-token prediction based on web text data is hitting a wall.

What if a time traveler told you that, by November 2026...

• AI models would have human-like fluid intelligence, thanks to a new paradigm: test-time induction (modern reasoning models).
• Not only would ARC 1 be saturated, but unreleased benchmarks 10x harder (ARC 2) and 100x harder (ARC 3) would be saturated too.
• Nearly all code would be written by AI, and models could one-shot complex codebases flawlessly.
• AI models would be solving multiple Millennium Prize problems.
• OpenAI's valuation would be 15x higher, and Anthropic's would be 85x higher.

And on top of all that...

• Nvidia would still hold ~80% of the AI compute market.
• Nvidia would have grown its revenue and earnings 4.5x.
• Nvidia would still be growing 75% a year.
• Nvidia would have even higher operating margins (67% vs. 65% back then).

Based on that information, straight from the future, would you have bought NVDA?

If you answered yes -- congrats. Today, 2.5 years later, you'd be down 5% on your investment (even more after inflation).

FSD v15 is starting to hit cars today, and I think this is a really BIG one.

Elon says the wider release is coming in December with the holiday update, calling it “something special.” This is the first wave, so if your car hasn’t received it yet, that’s normal fyi. 

The number everyone’s going to talk about is 25x.

Tesla says it's “25x better handling of safety critical cases,” while the release notes describe a 25x improvement in the critical intervention rate... that’s about situations where a driver needs to step in for safety. 

Tesla upgraded the vision encoder, the part of the AI that makes sense of what the cameras see. It’s shared with Robotaxi and Optimus, and Tesla says it was trained on millions of internet videos to help it understand more situations and learn more efficiently. A core piece of how the car, the robotaxi and the robot understand the world is now shared.

Then there’s Tesla Reality View.

The familiar gray driving display is now being replaced by a detailed view of the world around the car, created live from a virtual viewpoint above it. Ashok says the same model that drives the car also draws that scene. Arrows show the turns FSD plans to make, and pins show where it wants to park. 

Elon says you can tap a point in that view to tell the car where to go, with turn markers floating overhead like a video game. 

He says, “It’s like GTA" and the new visualization uses less computing power than the old one.

Tesla also lists better detection of road signs, small animals, debris, chains, potholes and finer details in the pavement. It also says v15 improves avoidance of deep standing water and handles speed better for your chosen profile, school zones, posted limits and bad weather.

Autoshift now uses FSD’s own predictions to choose the next gear. The cabin camera should also be able to monitor attention more often when you’re wearing a hat or sunglasses, and Tesla says it has made attention monitoring less strict in the faster driving profiles.

Navigation is changing at the beginning and end of the trip, too. It now learns from the routes the fleet prefers to take. Tesla plans to extend that approach to the entire route in later v15 updates... this first release covers departures and arrivals.

Parking also is more personal now. The car uses your parking history, and the map can show multiple spots at your destination so you can choose where you want to go. I like that, bc arriving at the right address and stopping where you actually want to be are two different things.

FSD can now also slow down when it detects a speed camera. Pressing the accelerator or increasing your speed profile cancels that slowdown. Cancel it twice at the same camera, and the car remembers that location and won’t automatically slow for that camera again. You can clear those saved locations if you like.

Bike Rack Mode lets you use FSD and Autosteer with a bike rack or similar hitch accessory attached. With that mode on, FSD pulls over near your destination and doesn’t reverse. Autopark, Summon, and backup chimes and warnings are disabled.

What gets me right now is that all of this is coming to cars people already own. The way the car understands its surroundings, handles the drive, chooses a parking spot and communicates with you is all about to change through a download.

You go to bed with your Tesla in the driveway. An update arrives overnight, and you can wake up to a different driving experience in the same car.

That still amazes me, that's the bread & butter of Tesla. 

Tesla just started shipping it today, can't wait to experience it!

Some random, unfiltered thoughts on AI and the market:

The gulf between “San Francisco” and “New York” has never been wider than it is right now 

AI is accelerating in capability, rapidly and in a way that is structurally changing, and in many ways upending, the nature of the firm and the fundamentals of capitalism

If that sounds extreme, consider that Anthropic has ~6,000 employees, Meta has 67,000, and both companies are worth ~$1.5T

Talk to your average startup and it’s clear that, given the opportunity to start from scratch, nobody is building their companies “the old way.” 

Talk to your average Fortune 500 company and it’s clear that getting an AI agent into production at scale is a Herculean task

Intelligence may not be the bottleneck, but firms built from the foundational assumption that intelligence is improving quickly in capability and price are scaling at a genuinely unbelievably velocity

There’s a reason Zuck wanted to fire 60% of many of the teams at his company, in large part likely out of frustration that he can’t start from scratch like his competitors had the luxury of doing

A structurally weaker Nvidia and OpenAI have minimal impact on the pace and impact of AI diffusing across the economy (“San Francisco”), but completely breaks the models built in “New York.” Hence the absolute freak-out these last few weeks. It was all priced to go perfectly and now things are not perfect 

But for the boots on the ground, AI will not slow down. And counterintuitively, economic weakness might accelerate diffusion. After all, tokens are much more fungible and flexible than people

Where does that leave us? I think firmly in the second phase of the AI build-out. Real value is being built in the app layer (though how defensible it is…TBD).  

Trying to predict the next bottleneck, or whether Washington does this or that other thing wrt policy, or exactly how many data centers get built out…who can say? Certainly not me. It’s not the bet I’m trying to make 

I’m looking at who wins from rapidly improving intelligence available at increasingly cheaper prices, and critically, which leaders are able to move with conviction into this new operating paradigm

That's an extraordinary amount of leverage in the system, and when markets start moving against investors, it can accelerate the selling pressure.

Unfortunately, even gold isn't immune. During a liquidity-driven selloff, investors often sell what they can, not necessarily what they want to. Gold can become a source of cash to cover margin calls and offset losses elsewhere.

URANIUM'S BIGGEST PROBLEM: THE MINES THAT DON'T EXIST YET

Utilities are covered today. But who supplies their reactors in 2030, 2032 or 2035?

That's the tension in a December 2025 interview with Justin Huhn of Uranium Insider. The argument is even more relevant today.

In the 2000s uranium boom, spot went from below $10 to about $135/lb. Some mining shares rose 10- to 100-fold before crashing.

Huhn believes this cycle could last longer because uranium supply responds painfully slowly to higher prices.

A deposit cannot become a mine just because spot reaches $100. It needs permits, financing, infrastructure, construction and a successful ramp-up. That takes years.

Demand is more predictable. Reactors need refuelling, life extensions add consumption, and Japan is restarting units. China is building reactors, buying overseas uranium and expanding fuel services. Data centres add another reason to preserve nuclear power.

THE CONTRACTING CLOCK IS TICKING

Utilities are comfortable near term. Further out, the picture changes dramatically.

Sprott, citing U.S. EIA data, estimates maximum U.S. utility contract coverage falls from about 98% in 2026 to 60% in 2030 and just 9% by 2033.

That isn't a fuel-shortage forecast. Utilities can sign contracts and draw inventories.

But it means substantial demand remains unsecured, just as the market is counting on mines that have yet to produce a pound.

CAMECO IS SHOWING ITS HAND

Huhn's interview quoted $75/lb spot and $86/lb long-term. Those figures are dated.

On November 20, spot was around $90/lb. TradeTech's October long-term indicator hit $99/lb.

More revealing is what Cameco says about contracts.

In its Q3 2026 call, Cameco described market-linked floors in the mid-to-high $70s, ceilings reaching $160, and three-digit prices on fixed-price portions.

These are contract terms, not a guarantee of $160 realized prices. But they show how much bargaining power disciplined producers have gained.

Huhn argues new major mines need sustained higher prices, potentially north of $100/lb, to justify financing and execution risk.

A short spike won't build a mine. Sustained incentive pricing might.

THE MINES THAT MUST DELIVER

NexGen's Arrow study forecasts 28.8 million lb a year for its first five years. Enormous supply from one mine.

Since Huhn spoke, NexGen secured its construction licence in March 2026 and started construction in June.

But construction isn't production. Shaft sinking, ground conditions, commissioning and ramp-up still matter. NexGen's own capital-cost estimate has already risen from about C$1.3 billion in its 2021 study to C$2.2 billion in a 2024 update.

And Arrow is only one mine. Future supply depends on other projects delivering as promised.

If they slip, utilities can't order replacement pounds from mines that don't exist.

THE FINANCIAL WILDCARD

Huhn also explains the carry trade: when forward uranium prices sufficiently exceed spot, traders can buy uranium, store it and sell it for future delivery.

That can support spot buying before utilities need delivery. It is not a guaranteed price floor.

Physical trusts and speculative traders could amplify a rally. They could amplify the downside too.

MY JUDGMENT

Huhn sees opportunities in beaten-down small uranium stocks. Perhaps. But this is where I'd be selective.

A shortage doesn't make every deposit profitable. Higher uranium prices won't fix bad contracts, excessive capex, weak management or repeated dilution.

Some stocks gained 1,000% or more in the last bull market. Others never rewarded shareholders.

The opportunity isn't simply to own uranium in the ground.

It's to own companies that turn it into profitable pounds before shareholders run out of patience and money.

Fast V-shaped recoveries form within days of capitulation, and corrections that hold support don’t become bear markets. From 6,900, the strongest past fast-V recoveries delivered 12-month gains of up to 38%, which puts 9,500 within reach. The timing adds to the case. 

The market is entering the sweet spot of the four-year presidential cycle, and the S&P has been higher a year after every midterm election since 1950.

Add a Fed pivot, and 10,000 is still in play. S&P 500 earnings will reach $450 in 2027, so the only argument is over the multiple. With the energy crisis passing, the 10-year Treasury yield will head to 4%, and the Greenspan Fed model then implies a multiple of 25.

Iranians are lining up for bread at 4 a.m., clutching cash and bank cards as fears of shortages and tighter access to subsidized bread deepen.

A circulating video shows a crowd pressing around a bakery before dawn, with captions saying people arrived early to buy bread before supplies ran out.

The scenes come amid reports of a quietly introduced “bread purchase management” system in Markazi, Khuzestan and Zanjan, with reports of expansion elsewhere and contradictory explanations from officials.

Under the reported rules, each person receives a monthly allowance equivalent to roughly 8 kilograms of subsidized flour, with purchases above that level charged at more than five times the subsidized rate.

That allowance works out to approximately 266 grams of flour per person a day, below the Health Ministry’s cited average consumption of roughly 333 grams.

Officials have disputed the “rationing” label, with some saying the changes target commercial purchases rather than ordinary households, but the opaque rollout has fueled confusion, queues and disputes at bakeries.

🚨 UPDATE sur Riemann et elle est énorme 

Hier, Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, annonçait avoir trouvé une preuve avec Claude. C'était une revendication, personne n'avait encore vérifié

Aujourd'hui, la Lean FRO et la Mathlib Initiative, les deux organisations derrière Lean et sa bibliothèque de maths, publient une déclaration commune : « We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct »

EN 24 HEURES !! 

Elles écrivent avoir « full confidence » dans la preuve et félicitent Alpöge

Après 167 ans cest le plus gros morceau des maths qui tombe, alors que tout le monde le voyait encore résister 30-50 ans. 

1. Ce qui a changé en 24h

Hier je vous disais que personne hors de son cercle n'avait confirmé que le code compile, ni que le théorème final dit exactement ce que dit l'hypothèse de Riemann

Les deux points sont réglés. Des dizaines de personnes ont recompilé la bibliothèque de leur côté et obtenu le même fichier de preuve, sans aucune erreur

Et l'énoncé démontré est bien celui de Mathlib, qui avait déjà été relu par des experts de Lean et de théorie des nombres

2. Comment ils ont vérifié

La preuve fait 17 millions de lignes de Lean et ne dépend directement que de Mathlib

La communauté a isolé l'énoncé de Riemann dans un fichier à part, qui n'importe que Mathlib, puis l'a comparé au théorème d'Alpöge avec deux outils indépendants, comparator et con-leche. Les deux confirment que c'est exactement le même énoncé

La preuve a ensuite été passée dans plusieurs vérificateurs, dont le noyau officiel de Lean, con-leche et con-ron, plus d'autres écrits par des tiers dans d'autres langages

Détail très fort : con-leche et con-ron ont eux-mêmes une preuve formelle qu'ils ne peuvent pas accepter une fausse preuve. Ça répond à la crainte d'une faille dans la logique de Lean que la preuve aurait pu exploiter

3. Claude des deux côtés

Andrew Sutherland, du MIT, publie tous ses fichiers de vérification. Et ses contrôles ont été lancés avec Claude Code

Sur sa page : les 175 187 modules compilent, la preuve n'utilise que les trois axiomes standard de Lean, et nanoda, un noyau indépendant écrit en Rust, accepte la preuve complète

Donc Claude a aidé à trouver la preuve, et Claude a aidé à la vérifier. Avec des outils indépendants à chaque étape. 

Pour le million du Clay Institute, les règles demandent une publication dans une revue reconnue, deux ans d'attente puis une acceptation générale par la communauté. Et Anthropic n'a fait aucune communication officielle

5. Ce que ça débloque

Comme je vous disait hier Des milliers de théorèmes commençaient par « si l'hypothèse de Riemann est vraie, alors… ». Ils tiennent maintenant sur une preuve vérifiée par machine

Pour les gros needs, Sutherland l'a déjà montré : en combinant la preuve avec une formalisation indépendante du critère de Robin, Lean démontre l'inégalité de Robin pour tout n > 5040, sans aucune mention de la fonction zêta

Le Lean blog conclut en attendant toute l'activité de la communauté pour expliquer les idées nouvelles de cette preuve. Les humains doivent maintenant comprendre ce que Claude et Alpöge ont trouvé, une première dans l’histoire 

L’ère de l’exponentielle vient de commencer, l’humanité entre dans un âge d’or

Dodd-Frank passed in July 2010 at 2,319 pages, and the banks wrote most of it. That sentence sounds conspiratorial until you read the lobbying disclosures. JPMorgan Chase spent $7.1 million lobbying during the bill's drafting phase. Goldman Sachs dispatched former employees throughout Treasury and the Fed, the same agencies tasked with writing the implementing regulations. The revolving door spun so fast it blurred into a single continuous institution.

Regulatory capture works like this: the regulator depends on the regulated industry for technical knowledge, career advancement, and institutional prestige. The industry therefore shapes the rules it nominally must follow. Dodd-Frank handed regulators 400 separate rulemaking requirements, each one a drafting opportunity for bank lawyers to define what their own compliance looks like.

The result protected you from nothing while erecting walls against anyone who might actually compete with Citigroup. Community banks collapsed from 7,085 in 2010 to under 4,500 by 2024, crushed under compliance costs that a trillion-dollar balance sheet absorbs casually but a $200 million regional bank cannot. The big got bigger. Concentration in the top five banks rose from 44% of total assets in 2010 to over 54% by 2026.

Complexity is a moat. Every page of regulation you cannot afford to decode is a page written against you and for the incumbents who can. Free market thinkers have identified this process more than a century ago, and the math never changes: when government controls the terms of market entry, the largest existing players control government.

Dodd-Frank's defenders said it disciplined Wall Street. Wall Street's stock prices recovered within three years, bonus pools swelled by 2013, and the five largest banks emerged structurally dominant in ways 2008 never threatened to produce on its own.

posts.name: Michael A. Arouet
posts.text:
Everyone is scratching his head after the recent market sell-off, but it’s really not that complicated. It’s pure math. Let’s take a look, shall we?

At their peaks, the major listed AI-exposed companies (Mag7 plus key chip, foundry, and infrastructure names) were worth roughly $28–32 trillion. Add Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation of about $1.2–1.5 trillion and an expected OpenAI post-IPO figure around $1.5 trillion, and the total sits in the $30–35 trillion range, approaching half the entire US equity market (recently ~$70–72 trillion).

Once a single theme absorbed that much capital, further large gains required either massive new inflows or more money pulled from everything else. At some point neither was available at the necessary scale. Expecting these names to double again from those peaks implied an incremental $30+ trillion of market value. The rest of the US market was only ~$40 trillion; global equity markets, bonds, and private capital held no unused liquidity of that magnitude ready for AI multiples. Leverage, retail flows, and foreign capital were already heavily committed.

The arithmetic simply stopped working. Prices could no longer be justified by any realistic path of further capital absorption. The pullback was the delayed recognition that the liquidity sucked into the trade had nowhere left to come from. It’s really that simple. Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations? That they would double again in three months?
